bio.en: Jeanne Grosser is the COO of Vercel, where she oversees marketing, sales, customer success, revenue operations, and field engineering, and she previously built Stripe's earliest sales team from the ground up as its Chief Product Officer.
bio.zh: Jeanne Grosser 是 Vercel 的首席运营官（COO），负责市场营销、销售、客户成功、营收运营和现场工程；此前她曾在 Stripe 担任首席产品官，从零搭建起 Stripe 最早的销售团队。

summary.en: Jeanne reframes go-to-market as a product problem, arguing that with AI intensifying competition, the ability to actually bring a product to market now matters more than ever. She explains that most enterprise buying is driven by avoiding pain and reducing risk rather than chasing upside, and that the buying experience itself is becoming a key differentiator between otherwise similar products. A standout idea is the 'go-to-market engineer'—a role on her team that lets them operate roughly ten times faster—and her litmus test that a great salesperson should be nearly indistinguishable from a product manager to engineers. The episode is a deep, tactical primer on segmentation, GTM process, tooling, and her hot takes on PLG, sales compensation, and sales hiring.
summary.zh: Jeanne 把“走向市场（go-to-market）”重新定义成一个产品问题，她认为在 AI 加剧竞争的当下，真正把产品推向市场的能力比以往任何时候都更重要。她解释说，企业采购大多是为了规避痛苦、降低风险，而不是为了追逐上行空间，而且当产品本身差异不大时，购买体验本身正在成为关键差异化因素。一个特别亮眼的想法是“走向市场工程师”（go-to-market engineer）这个角色——它让她的团队运转速度快了大约十倍——以及她那条“黄金标准”：优秀的销售在工程师面前应该几乎 indistinguishable（难以分辨）于产品经理。整期是对市场细分、GTM 流程、工具链的深入实战讲解，也包含了她对 PLG、销售薪酬和销售招聘的犀利观点。

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: I think there are two answers to this. Often what people think of is sort of the tip of the spear of what drives revenue, which is marketing and sales. Examples of this would be slightly differing segmentation frameworks, et cetera. turns.en: What has most changed in the world of go-to-market over the last few years? You've done this for a long time at Google, at Stripe, you built it for sales team, now you're doing that at Vercel. What's changed most in the skill and art of go-to-market?
turns.zh: 过去几年，上市领域发生的最大变化是什么？您在 Google、Stripe 已经这样做了很长时间，您为销售团队构建了它，现在您在 Vercel 也这样做了。进入市场的技巧和艺术变化最大的是什么？

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: There are a number of things. So when consumption-based business models started, I think you saw go-to-market shift into being meaningfully more consultative because often that first land was the very beginning of the journey and represented a very small percent of what you were ultimately going to do with that customer. And so you had to go from being transactional to a lot more. You had to more deeply understand what that customer was trying to do so you could align that ultimately to your product. I think that has played out that much more with an AI because right now everyone knows they need to change, but they don't necessarily know exactly what they need to change to, whether that's their customer-facing product or their internal productivity and workflows. And so I think you're seeing a lot more of go-to-market orgs leaning into the art of the possible best practices, helping you actually think things through as if they were a consultant. (00:09:52): And so one of the things you see more of right now is forward-deployed engineering, which on some level is kind of a rebrand of professional services but kind of not. And a big part of that is, hey, how do I actually get into your environment, ride alongside you better understand what you're trying to do and then help you actually bring the technology to life and learn a lot along the way. (00:10:18): Often you're not only making that customer successful, but you're then taking all of that back to your product and engineering organization to figure out, okay, what was generalizable that we ought to build into our offering versus what is something that ultimately is going to be more of a professional service in the fullness of time. So I think that has been a biggie, is actually just really getting embedded with your customer. And then unsurprisingly, I think bringing AI to bear on the sales process is another big one. And so you've seen the rise in probably the last 18 to 24 months of the go-to-market engineer, which different folks define slightly differently, but it's kind of bringing one technical prowess to bear on go-to-market in general so you can have a lot better tooling, data use, et cetera. And then two, increasingly bringing AI to bear as well to re-architect your workflows and also make it so that it's easier to have a personalized experience with customers but do so at scale.
turns.zh: 有很多事情。因此，当基于消费的商业模式开始时，我认为你会看到进入市场转变为更具咨询意义，因为通常第一块土地是旅程的开始，并且只占你最终要与该客户做的事情的一小部分。所以你必须从事务性转变为更多。您必须更深入地了解客户想要做什么，这样您才能最终将其与您的产品结合起来。我认为人工智能的作用更明显，因为现在每个人都知道他们需要改变，但他们不一定确切地知道他们需要改变什么，无论是面向客户的产品还是内部生产力和工作流程。因此，我认为您会看到更多的市场组织倾向于可能的最佳实践艺术，帮助您像顾问一样真正思考问题。 (00:09:52)：所以你现在看到更多的事情之一是前沿部署工程，这在某种程度上是专业服务的品牌重塑，但又不是。其中很大一部分是，嘿，我如何真正进入您的环境，与您一起更好地了解您想要做什么，然后帮助您真正将技术带入生活并在此过程中学到很多东西。 (00:10:18)：通常，您不仅要让客户取得成功，还要将所有这些带回您的产品和工程组织，以弄清楚我们应该在我们的产品中构建哪些通用内容，以及最终在时间成熟时提供更专业的服务。所以我认为这是一件大事，实际上只是真正融入你的客户。毫不奇怪，我认为将人工智能应用于销售流程是另一件大事。因此，您可能已经看到了过去 18 到 24 个月内上市工程师的崛起，不同的人对这一点的定义略有不同，但这总体上是一种技术实力对上市的影响，因此您可以拥有更好的工具、数据使用等。第二，越来越多地利用人工智能来重新构建您的工作流程，并使其更容易为客户提供个性化体验，但要大规模实现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay, let's follow the thread on this go-to-market engineer, so what was it like before and what are these engineers doing at companies?
turns.zh: 惊人的。好的，让我们跟随这位进入市场工程师的话题，了解一下之前的情况以及这些工程师在公司做什么？

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: So I think maybe an interesting story to tell. When I was at Stripe, we went to launch an outbound SDR function. So outbound prospecting and Stripe always ran lean. The company at that time had an operating principle which was efficiency is leverage. And so if you looked at the sales organization I was running, most companies out there probably would've had 30 SDRs and I was going to get four. So there's no way I was going to do the typical SDR approach and be successful. And so we thought to ourselves, okay, what can we do? We'll be super data-driven. And so we went and we started building project Rosland. Rosland is the scientist who originally mapped A-DNA. And what this was was effectively a company universe. So you can think of this as a massive database. Every row was a different company on the planet and every column was an attribute about that company that would help you sell to them in a more targeted fashion. (00:12:39): So at Stripe an example would be knowing that their business model was a marketplace was super helpful, because that would mean you wanted to sell Stripe Connect versus vanilla payments. And so the goal was basically, hey, can we create a mad Libs where I will come up with sort of a predefined email template, but 80% of it will be fill in the blank based on the different attributes of that customer. So if they're this industry or this business model, then pull this customer, reference this value prop, send it to this persona, not that. And we were trying to do this in 2017 and it was very hard and didn't actually totally work our ability to the false positive rate and we worked deeply with DSI and it just never really got there. And now that we're literally redoing here at Vercel as we speak and it actually works and you can bring AI to bear on it. (00:13:41): And so what's different is we now, I have a data scientist just like I did back in 2017, but I have a go-to-market engineer whereas before I just had someone in systems that was helping me configure outreach or sales off and my go-to-market engineer is helping me build an agent where we're coming up with, okay, well what's the human workflow that you would've done? And then how do you encode that using Vercel workflows as an example in actual code that's both deterministic and less so where an agent's going out and trying to replicate what a human might've done to produce that, fill in the blank, matlit.
turns.zh: 所以我想这可能是一个有趣的故事。我在Stripe的时候，我们去推出了出站SDR功能。因此，出站勘探和 Stripe 总是精益求精。当时公司的经营理念就是效率就是杠杆。因此，如果你看看我所运营的销售组织，大多数公司可能都会拥有 30 个 SDR，而我将获得 4 个。因此，我不可能采用典型的 SDR 方法并取得成功。所以我们心里想，好吧，我们能做什么？我们将超级数据驱动。所以我们开始建设罗斯兰项目。罗斯兰是最初绘制 A-DNA 图谱的科学家。这实际上是一个公司宇宙。所以你可以把它想象成一个巨大的数据库。每一行都是地球上不同的公司，每一列都是该公司的一个属性，可以帮助您以更有针对性的方式向他们销售产品。 (00:12:39)：在 Stripe，一个例子就是知道他们的商业模式是一个市场，这非常有帮助，因为这意味着你想出售 Stripe Connect 而不是普通支付。所以目标基本上是，嘿，我们可以创建一个疯狂的库，我将在其中提出一种预定义的电子邮件模板，但其中 80% 将根据该客户的不同属性来填补空白。因此，如果他们是这个行业或这种商业模式，那么就拉动这个客户，引用这个价值支柱，将其发送给这个角色，而不是那个角色。我们在 2017 年就试图做到这一点，这非常困难，实际上并没有完全发挥我们在误报率方面的能力，我们与 DSI 进行了深入合作，但它从未真正实现这一目标。现在，就在我们说话的时候，我们实际上正在 Vercel 重做，而且它确实有效，你可以让人工智能来实施它。 (00:13:41)：所以我们现在的不同之处在于，我有一名数据科学家，就像 2017 年一样，但我有一名市场工程师，而在此之前，我只是在系统中有人帮助我配置外展或销售，而我的市场工程师正在帮助我建立一个代理，我们正在想出一个代理，好吧，那么你会做什么人工工作流程？然后，如何使用 Vercel 工作流程作为实际代码中的示例对其进行编码，该代码既具有确定性，又不太确定代理外出并尝试复制人类可能所做的操作来生成该代码，填补空白，matlit。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love the ambition of that project. What is this, like eight years ago?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个项目的雄心壮志。这是什么，八年前的事了？

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love the big thinking there. We're going to map the entire universe of companies and then here's how we sell to them. And then just I'm trying to picture doing that without AI. It's like crazy to imagine trying that without AI and that's so much simpler to even imagine.
turns.zh: 我喜欢那里的大想法。我们将绘制整个公司的地图，然后我们将向他们销售产品。然后我试图想象在没有人工智能的情况下做到这一点。想象在没有人工智能的情况下尝试这一点简直是疯狂，而且想象起来要简单得多。

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: Well the thing that's amazing about that, just to geek out on a second, so I was working on that with a bunch of folks at Stripe on my team, obviously at a gentleman named Ben Salzman who went on to go to ZoomInfo and then actually recently just founded a go-to-market startup that is basically sort of productizing that concept of a company universe and then layering AI on it on top of it. And ultimately his view is actually AI will get to the point that you won't have to do outbound prospecting because it will just sort of company and product match. So it's fun to sort of see back in 2017 some of the folks doing that now work at OpenAI, they work at Anthropic, they also are doing GTM Eng. You've got him starting a totally AI native GTM company and then here I'm at Vercel trying to do the same.
turns.zh: 令人惊奇的是，我只是想花点时间来研究一下，所以我正在与 Stripe 团队的一群人一起研究这个问题，显然是在一位名叫 Ben Salzman 的绅士那里，他后来去了 ZoomInfo，然后实际上最近刚刚成立了一家进入市场的初创公司，基本上是将公司宇宙的概念产品化，然后将人工智能分层。最终他的观点是，人工智能实际上将达到这样的程度：你不必进行对外勘探，因为它只是将公司和产品进行匹配。因此，很高兴看到 2017 年的一些人现在在 OpenAI 工作，他们在 Anthropic 工作，他们也在做 GTM Eng。他创办了一家完全人工智能原生的 GTM 公司，而我在 Vercel 也试图做同样的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so what's cool is this is an emerging role, an emerging skill that I don't think a lot of people have recognized as something that is happening. So one example I'm hearing of what this role does is they automate outbound emails essentially and outbound outreach. They figure out, they write workflows and agents that figure out here's the company to go after, here's how we message them. Does that end up being kind of like an email that's custom designed and written for this prospect?
turns.zh: 好的，最酷的是这是一个新兴的角色，一种新兴的技能，我认为很多人都没有意识到它正在发生。因此，我听说这个角色的作用的一个例子是，他们基本上自动化出站电子邮件和出站外展。他们弄清楚了，他们编写了工作流程和代理，找出了要追寻的公司，这就是我们向他们发送消息的方式。这最终是否有点像为该潜在客户定制设计和编写的电子邮件？

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: That's one version. So it's broader than that really. Basically the full remit of GTM Eng will be to go through each of the different functions within go to market and break down all the different workflows that they do and then turn those into agents where AI is better placed than the human to do that task. So right now we started with actually inbound and are now moving to outbound because that workflow is most legible. And by legible I mean you can basically write it down. It's relatively replicable, mostly deterministic. So it's more likely that AI will do it well and we actually built the agent and then we keep a human in the loop. But from there we're starting to look at outbound and with an outbound we're starting more at the lower end of the market, where you tend to have slightly less customization because there's a single decision maker at the company. (00:16:56): But I think it'll take a while before we're able to really do that in a very large enterprise. There we might use an agent for research but maybe not all the way to actually send a message and that's just within the prospecting function. So other places that we're looking at this would be for install-based sales. So again there it's a little bit more deterministic because you've got awesome internal data on what a customer is and isn't using, what's the next best action? What's the thing they should get most value from? So that's where we're starting to map, hey, what does that ideal workflow look like? But basically you want to get to a state where as long as I've been in sales, they release these annual reports that help us all benchmark ourselves relative to one another. And one of the stats is what percent of time do your sellers actually spend in front of customers? (00:17:44): And for the 20 years I've been in sales, it's always been somewhere around 30% to 40%. So the minority of time is actually talking to other humans and I think we're getting to a point where with layering in agents, ideally we finally get salespeople to a point where they're actually spending 70% of their time interacting with humans and we can get the research, the follow-up, the things that are a little bit more rote and don't use the entirety of your human capacity done by an agent and then sort of unleash you to go deeper with your customers.
turns.zh: 那是一个版本。所以它实际上比这更广泛。基本上，GTM Eng 的全部职责将是遍历市场中的每个不同功能，并分解他们所做的所有不同工作流程，然后将它们转变为人工智能比人类更适合执行该任务的代理。因此，现在我们从实际入站开始，现在转向出站，因为该工作流程最清晰。我所说的清晰是指你基本上可以把它写下来。它相对可复制，大部分是确定性的。因此，人工智能更有可能做得很好，我们实际上构建了代理，然后让人类参与其中。但从那里我们开始关注出站，对于出站，我们更多地从低端市场开始，在那里你的定制化程度往往会稍低，因为公司只有一个决策者。 (00:16:56)：但我认为我们需要一段时间才能在一家非常大的企业中真正做到这一点。在那里，我们可能会使用代理进行研究，但可能不会一直实际发送消息，而这只是在勘探功能范围内。因此，我们正在考虑的其他地方是基于安装的销售。因此，它更具确定性，因为您拥有关于客户正在使用和未使用什么的出色内部数据，下一个最佳行动是什么？他们应该从什么事情中获得最大价值？这就是我们开始绘制的地方，嘿，理想的工作流程是什么样的？但基本上你想要达到这样一种状态：只要我从事销售工作，他们就会发布这些年度报告，帮助我们所有人相互比较自己。其中一项统计数据是，您的卖家实际在客户面前花费的时间百分比是多少？ (00:17:44)：在我从事销售工作的 20 年里，它一直在 30% 到 40% 左右。因此，少数时间实际上是在与其他人交谈，我认为我们已经达到了这样一个地步：通过代理分层，理想情况下，我们最终让销售人员真正花费 70% 的时间与人类互动，我们可以进行研究、跟进、一些更死记硬背的事情，而不是使用代理完成的全部人力能力，然后释放你与客户进行更深入的交流。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that this is such a great example of where AI is contributing in a very meaningful high ROI way, taking on all this work that people... like, you have to hire say 50 SDRs as you described to do and now you could do with a lot more. So it's a really cool example of leverage that AI gives you. One thing that I know a lot of people think about when they hear this is, okay, I'm going to get more of these really bad emails trying to pitch me on stuff and just like this isn't going to work. I can tell this is AI. What have you learned about how to do this where people actually receive emails that actually convert and do well?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这是一个很好的例子，说明人工智能以非常有意义的高投资回报率方式做出贡献，承担了人们......喜欢的所有这些工作，你必须像你描述的那样雇用 50 个 SDR，现在你可以做更多的事情。所以这是人工智能为你提供的杠杆作用的一个非常酷的例子。我知道很多人听到这个消息时都会想到的一件事是，好吧，我会收到更多这些非常糟糕的电子邮件，试图向我推销东西，就像这是行不通的。我可以说这是人工智能。对于如何做到这一点，让人们真正收到真正转化且效果良好的电子邮件，您学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: Our processes all always have human in the loop. And so basically where we'll start is we take a go to market engineer and we have them shadow the highest performing individual in that function. And so you can go and you shadow an SDR and you can see, oh wow, they've got seven tabs open. They're looking up the person on LinkedIn, they're reading about the company, they're doing chatGPT on this, they're looking in this database to get these sets of attributes. And so that's how you sort of inform the initial workflow. And then what we do is we let the agent make a call. So in the specific example with inbound, you have to determine whether or not you think the lead is likely to be qualified and then you have to determine what to say to it. And so we'll let the agent make those two calls. (00:19:44): It ultimately then does some deep research, pulls in a bunch of information from our databases and crafts a response, but we have a human review all of those and actually hit send. Now for us, we had 10 SDRs doing this inbound workflow and now we just have one that is effectively QA-ing the agent. The other nine we deployed on outbound, so we got to move them up the value chain. At some point I think we'll get to a place where we feel like, "Hey, the human reviewer is saying yes enough of the time that we feel confident that these will be on brand targeted, et cetera," but right now we're still trying to train the agent and it incorporates feedback on what we choose to reject, edit, et cetera.
turns.zh: 我们的流程始终都有人参与。因此，基本上我们首先要聘请一位市场工程师，让他们跟随该职能部门表现最好的个人。因此，您可以查看 SDR，然后您可以看到，哇哦，他们打开了七个选项卡。他们在 LinkedIn 上查找此人，他们正在阅读有关该公司的信息，他们正在对此进行 chatGPT，他们正在该数据库中查找以获取这些属性集。这就是您通知初始工作流程的方式。然后我们要做的就是让代理拨打电话。因此，在入站的具体示例中，您必须确定您是否认为潜在客户可能合格，然后您必须确定对该潜在客户说些什么。因此，我们将让代理拨打这两个电话。 (00:19:44)：它最终会进行一些深入的研究，从我们的数据库中提取大量信息并制定响应，但我们对所有这些进行了人工审查，然后实际上点击了发送。现在对于我们来说，我们有 10 个 SDR 来执行此入站工作流程，而现在我们只有一个对代理进行有效的 QA。另外九个我们部署在出站，所以我们必须将它们提升到价值链的上游。在某些时候，我认为我们会遇到这样的情况：“嘿，人类审阅者多次说“是”，我们有信心这些将成为品牌目标，等等，”但现在我们仍在尝试培训代理，它包含了有关我们选择拒绝、编辑等内容的反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you shared that it's already having a lot of impact. Like you said, you had 10 SDRs and now one can do the job of 10.
turns.zh: 您分享说它已经产生了很大的影响。就像你说的，你有 10 个 SDR，现在一个可以完成 10 个的工作。

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: So before we did that move, I mean the other thing that's just incredible about this is the person who built the lead agent was a single GTM engineer. He spent maybe 25-30% of his time on this. It was six weeks before we felt confident going from 10 to one. So it wasn't like this was a multi-quarter process, it actually moved super quickly and then again now we just sort of keep that agent manager working with the agent to get it to a point where we say, "Hey, we're ready to roll." Actually throughout the process we also tracked all of the KPIs that you typically would hold an SDR accountable to. We were looking at our lead to opportunity conversion rate, we're looking at the number of touches it takes the time to convert, and basically what we were able to do is hold that lead to opportunity conversion rate flat. So the agent is as good as our humans were, but it's actually condensed the number of touches it takes to convert because it's so much quicker at responding relative to leads inevitably sitting in the queue or coming in at nighttime and no one can get to it, that type of deal. So that's sort of when we knew it was ready to pull nine people off and shift them into outbound.
turns.zh: 因此，在我们采取这一行动之前，我的意思是另一件令人难以置信的事情是，构建首席代理的人是一位 GTM 工程师。他大概花了 25-30% 的时间在这上面。六周后，我们才有信心从 10 名增加到 1 名。所以这并不是一个需要多个季度的过程，它实际上进展得非常快，然后现在我们只是让代理经理与代理合作，以达到我们说的“嘿，我们准备好了”的程度。实际上，在整个过程中，我们还跟踪了您通常要求 SDR 负责的所有 KPI。我们正在研究潜在客户到机会的转化率，我们正在研究转换所需时间的接触次数，基本上我们能做的就是保持潜在客户到机会的转化率持平。因此，代理与我们的人类一样好，但它实际上浓缩了转换所需的接触次数，因为相对于不可避免地排在队列中或在夜间进入而没有人能够接触到的潜在客户，它的响应速度要快得多，这种类型的交易。因此，就在那时我们知道已经准备好将九个人撤走并将他们转移到出站。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's incredible. Okay, that's interesting. So you shift them to outbound. What I love about this is this SDR that is now doing this is, as you said, doing the things they enjoy more, they're talking to customers more, they're not doing all this kind of top of funnel rote work. I don't want to get into whole jobs AI discussion, but there's always been this talk about AI SDRs basically replacing SDRs. It feels like that's one thing where everyone's like this is a hundred percent going to be AI in the future. What I'm hearing here is it gives one Aster a lot more leverage and obviously you still need people running the show. Thoughts there? Just like do you think AI will replace all this at some point? And then I don't know, you don't need salespeople?
turns.zh: 那真是难以置信。好吧，这很有趣。所以你把它们转移到出站。我喜欢这个的是这个 SDR 现在正在做的事情，正如你所说，做他们更喜欢的事情，他们更多地与客户交谈，他们不做所有这些漏斗顶部的死记硬背的工作。我不想深入讨论人工智能的全部工作，但一直有关于人工智能 SDR 基本上取代 SDR 的讨论。感觉就像每个人都这样的一件事，就是未来百分百会成为人工智能。我在这里听到的是，它给了 Aster 更大的影响力，显然你仍然需要有人来主持这个节目。想法在那里？就像你认为人工智能会在某个时候取代这一切吗？然后我不知道，你们不需要销售人员吗？

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: I think on prospecting it can replace a fair amount because the average SDR wasn't doing overly sophisticated research in the first place. So where I, think the last part to go as I mentioned will be in deep enterprise prospecting where you can be at multiple layers in an org chart, you've got to pick between business lines, you've got to triangulate those. But I do think for the things that are more repetitive that often don't take that much time to learn and get ramped, AI will be good at that. And in my view, no one graduated from college and was like, "Yes, I just went to college for four years to become an SDR." It was more, "Okay, that's where you are forced to start." But I think the average SDR could have gone straight into outbound or straight into an SMB closing role. And so basically what we're just doing is shifting folks into something that uses more of their full capacity right out of the gates rather than sort of the forcing function of working your way up the totem pole.
turns.zh: 我认为在勘探方面它可以取代相当多的部分，因为一般的特别提款权首先并没有进行过于复杂的研究。因此，我认为正如我提到的，最后一部分将是深入的企业勘探，您可以在组织结构图中处于多个层次，您必须在业务线之间进行选择，您必须对这些业务线进行三角测量。但我确实认为，对于那些重复性较高、通常不需要太多时间来学习和掌握的事情，人工智能会很擅长。在我看来，没有人大学毕业后会说：“是的，我只是上了四年大学，就成为了一名特别提款权成员。”更多的是，“好吧，这就是你被迫开始的地方。”但我认为平均特别提款权可能会直接进入出站或直接进入中小企业结算角色。所以基本上我们所做的就是让人们从一开始就充分利用他们的全部能力，而不是强迫自己沿着图腾柱向上爬。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Since a lot of people listening to this aren't salespeople don't have a lot of background in sales, we've used this term SDR, there's also the term AE. Can you just help people understand what is an SDR, what do they do, what's an AE, and then what's the role above?
turns.zh: 惊人的。由于很多听这个的人都不是销售人员，没有太多的销售背景，所以我们使用了 SDR 这个术语，还有 AE 这个术语。您能否帮助人们了解什么是 SDR、它们的作用是什么、什么是 AE，以及上面的作用是什么？

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: Sure. So SDR is typically in charge of generating pipeline. They're meant to talk to prospective customers and get them to a point where it is worth investing time to run them through a sales process. You typically have two types of an SDR, have an inbound one. So this is where people come to your website, they fill out contact sales, they'll be the first call to make sure that it's actually worth a more expensive account executive to go and run a sales process or you then have outbound. So this is where when you want to grow faster than your inbound demand, they will go out and at this point you probably have a point of view on where you think you have product market fit. And so they will target that part of the market and try to drum up interest from folks who weren't otherwise raising their hand saying, I'd like to talk to you. (00:24:54): So that's sales development basically. Pipeline generation account executives are closers. So it's their job to take somebody from, "Okay, hey, I'm interested in learning about your solution, I have a legitimate problem. I potentially could make a decision," to, "I now believe that your product is the best in the market for me and I'm willing to pay for it." And then account executives, depending on the segments that your company sells into E.G. small business, mid-market enterprise, et cetera, they may work their way up the food chain from selling to a smaller company like an SMB or a startup. Those tend to be a little bit more of a transactional sale. You often have a single decision maker to then going into a mid-market or a commercial role where now maybe you have an economic buyer like somebody in finance and a technical buyer like somebody in engineering to getting into enterprise where you have procurement and you have committees and 10 people have to weigh in and you've got to help them figure out how to de-risk the fact that they're probably migrating from something so much more complicated coordination effort to sell.
turns.zh: 当然。因此，SDR 通常负责生成管道。他们的目的是与潜在客户交谈，让他们知道值得投入时间来引导他们完成销售流程。您通常有两种类型的 SDR，一种是入站类型。因此，这就是人们访问您的网站，他们填写联系销售人员的地方，他们将是第一个打电话的人，以确保确实值得聘请更昂贵的客户经理来运行销售流程，否则您就可以出站。因此，当您希望增长速度快于入境需求时，他们就会退出，此时您可能对自己的产品市场契合度有自己的看法。因此，他们将瞄准这部分市场，并试图引起那些没有举手说“我想和你谈谈”的人的兴趣。 (00:24:54)：这基本上就是销售发展。管道生成客户主管的关系更加密切。因此，他们的工作就是让某人从“好吧，嘿，我有兴趣了解你的解决方案，我有一个合法的问题。我可能会做出决定”，到“我现在相信你的产品对我来说是市场上最好的，我愿意为此付费。”然后是客户经理，具体取决于贵公司向 E.G. 销售的细分市场。小型企业、中端市场企业等，他们可能会从向中小型企业或初创公司等较小的公司销售产品，沿着食物链向上攀升。这些往往更像是一种交易性销售。你通常有一个决策者，然后进入中端市场或商业角色，现在你可能有一个经济买家，比如金融界的人，还有一个技术买家，比如工程界的人，进入企业，你有采购，你有委员会和 10 个人必须权衡，你必须帮助他们弄清楚如何降低风险，因为他们可能正在从更复杂的协调工作转向销售。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was extremely helpful. So SDR, pipeline generation, i.e., closer. Such a simple way of thinking about it. Okay, this is great. Going back to the GDM engineer, a few questions for people that may want to try this at their company, what scale do you think it makes sense to start hiring for this role? Having someone automate in the go-to-market process?
turns.zh: 这非常有帮助。所以SDR，管道生成，即更接近。这是一种简单的思考方式。好的，这太棒了。回到 GDM 工程师，有几个问题要问那些可能想在自己公司尝试这一职位的人，您认为开始招聘这个职位的规模是多少？让专人自动化进入市场流程？

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: What's interesting about this is it will force companies to be more rigorous about their sales process early. So often startups when they go from founder led sales to say, I'm going to have my first sales person, whether that's an actual account executive who has sales experience or your general athlete, wicked smart, who's going to go figure it out. Often founders will just say, "Okay, sales is showing up and talking to people. Isn't that what I just did for the last couple of years?" But actually sales is more than that. It's a skill just like writing code as a skill or building a financial model as a skill, it's about discovery. So asking all the right questions that help you identify challenges in pain, willingness to pay, et cetera, and then going through a process to handle those objections and showcase where are you at enough value such that somebody ultimately wants to hand over some money. (00:27:24): So often startups will get, particularly ones with strong product market fit to pretty significant scale without really having a replicable process. And you can't really apply go to market engineering unless you actually have a point of view on what best practice should look like. And so I think basically this is going to force folks to have more of a playbook out of the gates, what's working, what's not? Can I document it? Do I have content for the different parts of the sales process? And then once you do that, which maybe 10 people is a good size and scale for that, ostensibly a GTM engineer can come in and turn that into an agent. You could also argue that if you're a founder who wants to bring in a general athlete profile and that person is technically minded, that you could have a hybrid AE GTM engineer who figures out what their best practice is and then tries to turn that into an agent that's riding alongside them and making them more effective as well. (00:28:26): So I don't know that I have a point of view yet on what's the optimal size and scale, but I forever have given founders the advice that you often want to bring in revenue operations, which is basically the analytical arm of sales earlier than you think because having data, having process is actually what gives you insights as a founder into what is and isn't working. And so I would argue just like it's a good idea to have that sooner than later, increasingly it'll probably be a good idea to have GTM engine and be looking to bring agents to bear on your process at the outset.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，它将迫使公司尽早对其销售流程更加严格。通常，初创公司在创始人领导销售时会说，我将拥有我的第一位销售人员，无论是具有销售经验的实际客户主管，还是聪明绝顶的普通运动员，他们都会去解决这个问题。通常创始人只会说：“好吧，销售人员出现并与人们交谈。这不是我过去几年所做的吗？”但实际上销量远不止于此。这是一种技能，就像编写代码作为一种技能或构建财务模型作为一种技能一样，它是关于发现的。因此，提出所有正确的问题，帮助你识别痛苦、支付意愿等方面的挑战，然后通过一个流程来处理这些异议​​，并展示你的价值足以让某人最终愿意交出一些钱。 (00:27:24)：初创公司经常会遇到这样的情况，特别是那些拥有强大的产品市场、规模相当大的公司，但实际上没有可复制的流程。除非您确实对最佳实践应该是什么样子有自己的看法，否则您无法真正应用市场工程。所以我认为基本上这将迫使人们拿出更多的剧本，什么有效，什么无效？我可以记录下来吗？我是否有销售流程不同部分的内容？然后一旦你这样做了，也许 10 个人是一个很好的规模，表面上 GTM 工程师可以进来并将其变成一个代理。你也可以说，如果你是一位创始人，想要引入一般运动员的资料，并且该人具有技术头脑，那么你可以拥有一名混合 AE GTM 工程师，他找出他们的最佳实践是什么，然后尝试将其转变为与他们并肩作战的代理，并使他们更加高效。 (00:28:26)：所以我不知道我对什么是最佳规模和规模有自己的看法，但我一直向创始人提供建议，即你经常想要引入收入运营，这基本上是比你想象的更早的销售分析部门，因为拥有数据、拥有流程实际上可以让你作为创始人洞察什么是有效的，什么是无效的。因此，我认为，就像迟早拥有它是一个好主意一样，拥有 GTM 引擎并在一开始就寻求让代理来影响您的流程也可能是一个好主意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: While we're on this topic, just a quick tangent, the advice for hiring your first salesperson that I usually hear is wait until you're around a million in ARR. When you have a repeatable process, you can teach someone anything there. Does that seem right? What would you recommend?
turns.zh: 当我们谈论这个话题时，只是简单切题一下，我通常听到的雇用第一位销售人员的建议是等到你的 ARR 达到 100 万左右。当你有一个可重复的过程时，你可以在那里教别人任何东西。这看起来对吗？你会推荐什么？

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: Yeah, I think that seems about right. I do think as a founder you want to stay deeply connected to customers and get it to a scale and get it to a point where you use the word, there's some repeatability there. I think that's one of the things that not all founders get right is founders are incredible salespeople. They convinced a VC angel investors to fork over a bunch of money, so clearly they're going to inspire people to buy. But if you're getting to a million in ARR and the set of customers you have look nothing like one another, you still have very much like an evangelist sale, very much founder led sale versus if you can say, "Hey, I now have an ICP here, or ideal customer profile, e.g something you can write down. We are good. Our product fits with startups with less than a hundred employees who are typically building SaaS applications," something like that. (00:30:14): Then you're probably ready to hand over the reins. And then what founders have to remember is to actually hand over the reins. So you've got to enable the person who comes in, what is it that you're doing effectively, what's your content, what are the discovery questions you are asking? How are you handling objections so you can transition that knowledge but also don't handle them over entirely. You want to stay connected to the customer because you still have a fair amount of R&D to do to figure out where is the product next going to resonate, where are you getting stock as you scale, etc.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为这似乎是正确的。我确实认为，作为创始人，你希望与客户保持深入的联系，并将其扩大到一定程度，并达到你使用这个词的程度，那里有一些可重复性。我认为并非所有创始人都做对的事情之一是创始人是令人难以置信的销售人员。他们说服了一位风险投资天使投资者投入了一大笔钱，所以显然他们会激励人们购买。但是，如果你的 ARR 达到 100 万，并且你拥有的客户群看起来彼此毫无相似之处，那么你的销售仍然很像传道者销售，很大程度上是创始人主导的销售，而不是你可以说，“嘿，我现在这里有一个 ICP，或者理想的客户档案，例如你可以写下来的东西。我们很好。我们的产品适合员工少于 100 人的初创公司，他们通常构建 SaaS 应用程序，”之类的话。 (00:30:14)：那么您可能已经准备好交出控制权了。然后创始人必须记住的是真正交出控制权。所以你必须让进来的人知道你正在有效地做什么，你的内容是什么，你要问的发现问题是什么？你如何处理异议，以便你可以转移这些知识，但也不要完全处理它们。您希望与客户保持联系，因为您仍然需要进行大量的研发工作，以弄清楚产品接下来会在哪里引起共鸣，随着规模的扩大，您在哪里获得库存等等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To close the loop on the go-to-market engineer, what's the profile of the ideal go-to-market engineer, may be your first.
turns.zh: 为了关闭市场推广工程师的循环，理想的市场推广工程师的个人资料可能是您的首要考虑。

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: What we have found works really well is somebody who does have go-to-market experience. So at Vercel, our first three go-to-market engineers we're actually sales engineers. So Vercel hires very technical sales engineers, all of them were front end developers before they decided they wanted to get into sales. And so we just said, "Hey, three of you, congrats." You're now founding members of our GTM Eng team. And the thing that works well there is you do understand aspects of what is good GTM, what does a process look like? It's been really interesting actually. So the gentleman who runs GTM Eng for me, we were going through this lead agent and QA-ing it. And so I'm going and I'm looking at some of the responses that we've ultimately had the lead agent send and realized, "Oh, I wouldn't have sent that and that's because I have 20 years of sales experience and we modeled the lead agent off our best person, but our best person who has two years of sales experience." So it actually is important to understand the art and the science of sales and how you bring best practice to bear. Either you've done it and so you know some best practice or you're going to geek out on sales, read a bunch of books, learn a thing or two, and try to incorporate some of those into your agent development.
turns.zh: 我们发现真正有效的是那些具有进入市场经验的人。因此，在 Vercel，我们的前三名市场推广工程师实际上是销售工程师。因此，Vercel 聘请了技术含量很高的销售工程师，他们在决定进入销售行业之前都是前端开发人员。所以我们只是说，“嘿，你们三个，恭喜。”您现在是我们 GTM 工程团队的创始成员。在那里运作良好的事情是你确实了解什么是好的 GTM，流程是什么样的？实际上这真的很有趣。因此，为我管理 GTM Eng 的那位先生，我们正在审查这位首席代理并对其进行质量检查。所以我要去查看我们最终让首席代理人发送的一些回复，并意识到，“哦，我不会发送这些回复，那是因为我有 20 年的销售经验，我们以我们最好的人为原型，但我们最好的人有两年的销售经验。”因此，了解销售的艺术和科学以及如何运用最佳实践实际上很重要。要么你已经完成了，所以你知道一些最佳实践，要么你将深入研究销售，阅读一堆书籍，学习一两件事，并尝试将其中的一些内容纳入你的代理开发中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really interesting. So come from the sales side, not from the engineering side. And I imagine this is such a cool opportunity for salespeople to do something completely different and move closer to engineering.
turns.zh: 这真的很有趣。所以来自销售方面，而不是来自工程方面。我认为这对于销售人员来说是一个非常酷的机会，可以做一些完全不同的事情并更接近工程。

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: Yeah, I mean we're having a lot of fun with it. At Vercel in particular, we basically get to be customer zero. So everything that we're building with agents, we're building on Vercel's AI cloud. So these agents now have multiple steps that they go through. So we're using Vercel's workflow SDK and workflow offering. We use the AI gateway to call the different models that we use to do deep research or other enrichment that we do. So for us it's great because we basically sort of bang on everything the engineering team is building and get to go be a discerning customer before we actually get it out the door to real customers.
turns.zh: 是的，我的意思是我们玩得很开心。特别是在 Vercel，我们基本上成为零客户。因此，我们使用代理构建的所有内容都是在 Vercel 的 AI 云上构建的。因此，这些代理现在要经历多个步骤。因此，我们使用 Vercel 的工作流程 SDK 和工作流程产品。我们使用人工智能网关来调用我们用来进行深入研究或其他丰富工作的不同模型。所以对我们来说，这很棒，因为我们基本上对工程团队正在构建的所有东西都进行了猛烈的攻击，并在我们真正将其交付给真正的客户之前成为一个挑剔的客户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a fun time to be alive. I could tell the fun that you guys are having, just from the way you describe it. (00:33:29): Stripe handles the massive scale and complexity of many of the world's fastest growing enterprises, including 78% of the Forbes AI 50 and more than half of the Fortune 100 enterprises like Atlassian, Figma and Urban Outfitters use Stripe to create fully branded and customized checkout pages with access to more than 125 global payment methods. There's a reason I've had more leaders from Stripe on this podcast than any other company. They know how to build great products that scale and that people love. And Stripe is a lot more than payments. They've also got a category leading billing solution and a highly optimized checkout experience built specifically to increase your checkout conversion. Join the ranks of industry leaders like Salesforce, OpenAI and Pepsi that are using Stripe to grow faster and to grow the world's GDP, learn how Stripe can help your business grow at Stripe.com. Zooming out a little bit in terms of you mentioned tools and tools that you use. I'm curious just what are kind of the state of the art tools within the go-to-market stack that you love that you'd recommend?
turns.zh: 活着真是太有趣了。从你们描述的方式我就能看出你们玩得很开心。 (00:33:29)：Stripe 能够处理全球许多发展最快的企业的大规模和复杂性问题，其中包括 78% 的福布斯 AI 50 强企业以及超过一半的财富 100 强企业（例如 Atlassian、Figma 和 Urban Outfitters），使用 Stripe 创建完全品牌化和定制的结账页面，并可访问超过 125 种全球支付方式。在这个播客中，来自 Stripe 的领导者数量比任何其他公司都多，这是有原因的。他们知道如何打造可扩展且人们喜爱的优秀产品。 Stripe 的用途远不止于支付。他们还拥有类别领先的计费解决方案和专门为提高结帐转化率而构建的高度优化的结帐体验。加入 Salesforce、OpenAI 和 Pepsi 等使用 Stripe 实现更快增长并提高全球 GDP 的行业领导者行列，在 Stripe.com 上了解 Stripe 如何帮助您的业务发展。稍微缩小一下您提到的工具和您使用的工具。我很好奇您喜欢推荐哪些最先进的上市工具？

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: Well, so I'm going to have an interesting answer to this, so I'll give you one. And it's not state-of-the-art per se, although I don't mean that disparagingly, it's just that it's been around for a while now and a lot of folks use it, but I think Gong has gotten just meaningfully more interesting in the last year. And then second half of my question I will get into, I think the calculus on build versus buy is changing. So all right, Gong. Gong is incredible because you can run agents against it now. So we take all of our Gong transcripts and we dump them into an agent called the deal-bott, and that deal-bott then can do a bunch of things. So the first thing we had it do was lost opportunity review. So we had just finished Q2, we had a list of our top losses for the quarter sorted by deal size, and we ran it against that and it was incredibly interesting. (00:35:39): So the biggest loss that quarter according to the account executive was lost on price. And when you ran the agent over every Slack interaction, every email, every GONG call, it said actually you lost because you never really got in touch with an economic buyer. And when you talked to somebody about ROI and total cost of ownership, it was clear from their reaction that they didn't really buy your mass. And so really the reason we lost was an inability to demonstrate value, which upon reflection I've got work to do to build out how we quantify the value of Vercel, which actually is very easily quantifiable. It's one of the things I love about selling this product, but we got to codify that for the go-to-market team. So that was incredibly interesting and now we run it against all of our lost opportunities and actually do a much better job of categorizing why it was we really, really lost. (00:36:38): And then either feeding that back into the engineering team or back into marketing sales leadership on, hey, where are we falling short in the sales process? And so that was awesome, but then we're like, well, it's not very fun to lose, so why don't we pull that forward? And so we went from lost bot to deal-bott and now the deal-bott is running in real time and we basically feed insights into Slack. Vercel is incredibly heavy users of Slack, so we have a channel for every single customer, either opportunity or existing one. And so now we're feeding insights into that Slack channel which is, "Hey, you're this far into the sales process and you haven't talked to an economic buyer, you should think about that." Or, "Hey, you just got off that call with an economic buyer, didn't sound like it went that well. Here's some things to consider and how you might follow-up." (00:37:34): And last thing before I pause, the other thing that's really interesting and how we're using this too is we are in this moment where I have never seen an iteration velocity exists now in my career. My 20 plus year career has all been in tech. And so for go-to-market teams, that's really hard. If you are launching something every other day, the ability to be enabled on that is actually quite challenging. And so this bot agent is now also letting us, where we're starting to go with it is we'll release something, we'll do our best to enable the team, then we'll go run the agent across calls, interactions, and we'll diagnose where we did a bad job of objection handling, where we're getting stuck. And then at the end of the week we can have a huddle and say, okay, what are all the places that our agent would suggest we aren't selling effectively? (00:38:34): And then almost like an engineering team, we'll now run sprints, which is like those are just bugs. They're bugs in your go-to-market process, so you should not have them. And by the next week we're going to add content to our objection handling to guide. We're going to add content to a discovery guide, we're going to figure out something we need to change about our demo, so on and so forth. So that's early. That's a little bit of a preview, but that's where we're talking about taking things right now within our go-to-market orgs.
turns.zh: 好吧，所以我对此会有一个有趣的答案，所以我会给你一个。它本身并不是最先进的，尽管我并不是贬低它，只是它已经存在了一段时间并且很多人使用它，但我认为 Kong 在去年变得更加有趣了。然后我将进入问题的后半部分，我认为构建与购买的计算正在发生变化。好吧，龚。龚是不可思议的，因为你现在可以运行特工来对抗它。因此，我们将所有的Gong 记录转储给一个名为deal-bott 的代理，然后那个deal-bott 就可以做很多事情。所以我们让它做的第一件事就是回顾失去的机会。所以我们刚刚完成第二季度，我们有一个按交易规模排序的本季度最大亏损清单，我们将其与此进行比较，这非常有趣。 (00:35:39)：据客户主管称，该季度最大的损失是价格损失。当你让代理检查每一次 Slack 互动、每封电子邮件、每一次 GONG 电话时，它实际上说你输了，因为你从未真正与经济买家取得联系。当您与某人谈论投资回报率和总体拥有成本时，从他们的反应中可以清楚地看出，他们并没有真正购买您的产品。因此，我们失败的真正原因是无法展示价值，经过反思，我需要做一些工作来确定如何量化 Vercel 的价值，而 Vercel 的价值实际上很容易量化。这是我喜欢销售该产品的原因之一，但我们必须将其编入市场团队。所以这非常有趣，现在我们针对所有失去的机会进行了分析，并且实际上更好地对我们真正失去的机会进行了分类。 (00:36:38)：然后要么将其反馈给工程团队，要么反馈给营销销售领导层，嘿，我们在销售过程中哪些地方存在不足？这真是太棒了，但我们会想，好吧，输球并不是一件很有趣的事，所以我们为什么不把它向前推进呢？因此，我们从丢失的机器人转变为交易机器人，现在交易机器人正在实时运行，我们基本上将见解输入到 Slack 中。 Vercel 是 Slack 的重度用户，因此我们为每一位客户（无论是机会客户还是现有客户）提供了一个渠道。所以现在我们正在向 Slack 渠道提供洞察，“嘿，你已经进入销售流程了这么远，而且你还没有与经济买家交谈过，你应该考虑一下。”或者，“嘿，你刚刚与一位经济买家通了电话，听起来进展不太顺利。这里有一些需要考虑的事情以及你可以如何跟进。” (00:37:34)：在我暂停之前的最后一件事，另一件真正有趣的事情以及我们如何使用它是，我们正处于我的职业生涯中从未见过迭代速度的时刻。我 20 多年的职业生涯都在科技领域。因此，对于进入市场的团队来说，这确实很难。如果您每隔一天就启动一些东西，那么启用它的能力实际上是相当具有挑战性的。所以这个机器人代理现在也让我们这么做，我们开始做的是我们将发布一些东西，我们将尽最大努力为团队提供支持，然后我们将在呼叫、交互中运行代理，我们将诊断我们在异议处理方面做得不好的地方，我们在哪里陷入困境。然后在周末，我们可以聚在一起讨论，好吧，我们的代理商会建议我们哪些地方销售效果不佳？ (00:38:34)：然后就像一个工程团队一样，我们现在将运行冲刺，就好像这些只是错误一样。它们是您的上市流程中的错误，因此您不应该拥有它们。到下周，我们将在异议处理中添加内容以提供指导。我们将向发现指南添加内容，我们将找出需要对演示进行更改的内容，等等。所以说还早。这只是一个预览，但这就是我们现在正在讨论的在我们的市场营销组织中采取行动的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Jeanne, you're blowing my mind in so many ways, it just sounds so fun and just you guys are going to win is what I'm feeling when I hear all this. Incredible. What I love about this is this AI tool, this agent you built sees things that humans were not seeing. The fact that you were surprised of just like this is a completely different conclusion is such a big deal. This is the whole promise of ai, it's going to do things we aren't even thinking about or capable of.
turns.zh: 珍妮，你在很多方面都让我大吃一惊，这听起来很有趣，当我听到这一切时，我的感受就是你们会赢。极好的。我喜欢这个人工智能工具，你构建的这个代理可以看到人类看不到的东西。令你惊讶的是，这是一个完全不同的结论，这真是一件大事。这就是人工智能的全部承诺，它将做我们想不到或没有能力做的事情。

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: It is. We had a really interesting, one of the things we're doing at Vercel, we have an AI cloud, so people use that to put AI-native features into their customer-facing applications, but they're also using it to build internal applications to improve productivity or outcomes. And we are talking to a very large airline and that airline obviously gets tons and tons of support queries. So of course they would want to go apply AI to hey, how can we have AI answer these so that our cost to support goes down, sort of the obvious thing. But the more interesting conversation was actually with one of the C-level executives who said, we also actually transcribe every single one of those support calls. And so what I really want to know is why are they calling and how do I make it so that fewer people call the next week? And so again, this is now with AI, you can rapidly go through all of that content and actually be able to much more quickly than having a human in your CRM sort of pick some status why it was that folks were calling the airline this week and what if anything you can do to make it less the case next week.
turns.zh: 这是。我们在 Vercel 正在做的事情之一非常有趣，我们拥有 AI 云，因此人们使用它来将 AI 原生功能放入面向客户的应用程序中，但他们也使用它来构建内部应用程序以提高生产力或结果。我们正在与一家非常大的航空公司交谈，该航空公司显然收到了大量的支持查询。所以他们当然想要应用人工智能来嘿，我们怎样才能让人工智能回答这些问题，以便我们的支持成本下降，这是显而易见的事情。但更有趣的对话实际上是与一位 C 级高管的对话，他说，我们实际上还转录了每一个支持电话。所以我真正想知道的是他们为什么打电话，以及我如何才能减少下周打电话的人？再说一次，现在有了人工智能，你可以快速浏览所有这些内容，实际上比在你的 CRM 中让人工更快地选择一些状态，为什么人们这周给航空公司打电话，以及如果你能做些什么来减少下周的情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine many people hearing this are like, "I need one of these deal-botts and lost bots." These are all internal products that you all built?
turns.zh: 我想很多人听到这句话都会想，“我需要这些交易机器人和丢失的机器人之一。”这些都是你们内部做的产品吗？

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything that you've learned about making them this good? Any tips you can share of here's how to make a really good bot for sales?
turns.zh: 您是否学到了什么才能让它们变得如此出色？您可以分享一下如何制作真正优秀的销售机器人的任何技巧吗？

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: Yes, so actually that's the second half of my answer that I forgot.
turns.zh: 是的，实际上这是我忘记的答案的后半部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's perfect.
turns.zh: 那很完美。

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: Which is sort of like bill versus buy calculus. So I think one of our learnings is that it's not that hard to build these agents and they aren't that expensive either. So I mentioned the lead agent that was a six-week process with one human, a third of his time, that deal-bott, the lost bot version was two days basically we riffed on it, he had it 40 hours later. Now we're continuing to refine it for the other things I mentioned. And what's also interesting about them is they for better or for worse for Vercel, but that lead agent which runs full stack on Vercel, will cost us about a thousand dollars to run for the entire year. If you remember I told you we had 10 people in the SDR function, so I'm paying well over a million dollars for that from a salary perspective. (00:41:57): I got that down to one. And then behind that I have a lead agent that costs a thousand bucks. So that's like a 90%-plus reduction in total cost there. And there's lots of software for agents out there right now. And I think one of the things we're learning is because this whole space is so nascent, often your own esoteric context, your content, your workflow is really key to unlocking the power of the agent. And so I think there's real value in experimenting with your own internal agent development. We may ultimately end up on better integrated agent platforms in the fullness of time, or we may find that the CIO increasingly goes from a procurer of software to a builder of software and you'll have an AI internal platform with a thousand agents running across your org. I'm not really sure yet. But I certainly think there's value in trying it yourself because you may find that it's meaningfully easier than you think and you get returns pretty quickly.
turns.zh: 这有点像账单与购买的计算。所以我认为我们的经验之一是构建这些代理并不难，而且它们也不是那么昂贵。所以我提到了首席代理，这是一个人的六周过程，三分之一的时间，那个交易机器人，丢失的机器人版本基本上是我们重复的两天，他在 40 小时后得到了它。现在我们正在继续针对我提到的其他内容进行完善。同样有趣的是，它们对 Vercel 来说是好是坏，但在 Vercel 上运行全栈的首席代理将花费我们大约 1000 美元来运行一整年。如果您还记得我告诉过您，我们有 10 名 SDR 职能人员，那么从薪资角度来看，我为此支付的费用远远超过 100 万美元。 (00:41:57)：我把它归结为一。然后我有一个花费一千美元的首席经纪人。因此，总成本降低了 90% 以上。现在有很多针对代理的软件。我认为我们正在学习的一件事是因为整个空间是如此新生，通常你自己深奥的背景、你的内容、你的工作流程确实是释放代理力量的关键。因此，我认为尝试自己的内部代理开发具有真正的价值。随着时间的推移，我们最终可能会得到更好的集成代理平台，或者我们可能会发现 CIO 越来越多地从软件采购者转变为软件构建者，并且您将拥有一个人工智能内部平台，在您的组织中运行着一千个代理。我还不太确定。但我当然认为自己尝试是有价值的，因为你可能会发现它比你想象的要容易得多，而且你很快就能得到回报。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I'm hearing here is that you're finding that there are not tools out there to plug and play. The alpha is essentially in building your own stuff.
turns.zh: 所以我在这里听到的是，您发现没有可以即插即用的工具。阿尔法本质上是构建你自己的东西。

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: I think that's partially true, and I think because you also have all these tools proliferating right now, you get into the perennial problem where you wind up with 20 of them to do the 20 jobs to be done basically, rather than an integrated platform that's doing all of them. I'm hearing this a lot actually when I'm talking to customers right now where their biggest issue in deploying AI is actually just getting through procurement and it's because got an AI mandate, you kind of have a blank check. I recently heard the term of instead of ARR, it's ERR, which is experimental run rate revenue, which is to say everyone's out there sort of, Hey, we're going to give this thing a go for a year and then TBD on whether or not we keep it. But basically you're having to procure 20 different things. Most things are getting off the ground and so they're solving something relatively narrow and that'll change in the fullness of time. But I do think there's an opportunity to figure out, hey, where do I likely have a more specific workflow internally. For that it might be worth building your own agent and then maybe for the things that are a little bit more generalizable, you go get something off the shelf.
turns.zh: 我认为这部分是正确的，而且我认为因为现在所有这些工具都在激增，所以您会遇到一个长期存在的问题，即最终需要使用其中的 20 个工具来完成基本上要完成的 20 项工作，而不是一个可以完成所有这些工作的集成平台。事实上，当我现在与客户交谈时，我经常听到这样的说法，他们部署人工智能的最大问题实际上只是通过采购，这是因为获得了人工智能授权，你就拥有了一张空白支票。我最近听到的术语不是ARR，而是ERR，这是实验性的运行率收入，也就是说每个人都在说，嘿，我们将尝试这个东西一年，然后待定我们是否保留它。但基本上你必须采购 20 种不同的东西。大多数事情都在顺利进行，所以他们正在解决一些相对狭窄的问题，随着时间的推移，这些问题将会发生变化。但我确实认为有机会弄清楚，嘿，我内部可能在哪里有更具体的工作流程。为此，可能值得构建自己的代理，然后对于更通用的东西，您可以去购买现成的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there any platforms or tools that you want to shout out that allow you to build these agents so quickly? I know they sit on Versel, so shout out Vercel. But just anything that you point people to you to... These SDR, these GTM engineers, they're former salespeople. Are they learning to code? Are they byte coding these agents? How does that work?
turns.zh: 是否有任何您想要大声疾呼的平台或工具可以让您如此快速地构建这些代理？我知道他们坐在 Vercel 上，所以大声喊出 Vercel。但只要你向人们介绍你的任何事情……这些 SDR、这些 GTM 工程师，他们都是前销售人员。他们正在学习编码吗？他们对这些代理进行字节编码吗？这是如何运作的？

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: So our sales engineers all have CS degrees. So they were engineers in a sales capacity, so they're writing code and actually these agents, they're building directly on Versel. So you get the AI gateway that lets you call different models. You have a sandbox if you're running untrusted code, you've got workflows that let you build the process. You've got fluid compute, which lets you really efficiently use compute when you only need it. So we're just sort of building it from the ground up here. Again, it's not that hard. Now you do need to write code for that. Certainly there are a lot of vibe coding tools out there that also give you more workflow builders that are somewhere between fully WYSIWYG, almost like drag and drop and a little bit more code forward. So you've got a bunch out there along those lines. But I do think we've sort of found one of the reasons actually the GTM Eng team at Versel can build these agents so easily is because the Versel platform is making it that easy to use our framework to find infrastructure and get that agent onto into production very rapidly.
turns.zh: 所以我们的销售工程师都有CS学位。所以他们是具有销售能力的工程师，所以他们正在编写代码，实际上这些代理，他们直接在 Versel 上构建。这样您就可以获得可以调用不同模型的 AI 网关。如果您正在运行不受信任的代码，那么您就有了一个沙箱，您就有了可以构建流程的工作流程。您拥有流畅的计算，这让您可以在仅需要时真正有效地使用计算。所以我们只是从头开始构建它。再说一遍，这并不难。现在您确实需要为此编写代码。当然，有很多氛围编码工具也为您提供了更多介于完全所见即所得之间的工作流构建器，几乎就像拖放和更多的代码转发。所以你已经有很多这样的人了。但我确实认为我们已经找到了 Versel 的 GTM Eng 团队实际上可以如此轻松地构建这些代理的原因之一，因为 Versel 平台使我们可以轻松地使用我们的框架来查找基础设施并非常快速地将代理投入生产。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a neat, unfair advantage you all have to do this stuff.
turns.zh: 你们做这件事是多么巧妙、不公平的优势啊。

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: Yes, it is fun to... I mean, I do think this company is better than any I've seen at eating its own dog food and just everyone is constantly, we say Versel builds Versel with Versel. So you're just always looking for ways to, Hey, how can we use our product to go do what we need to do? And as a result, either understand then what a customer would want or what's missing from our product that we could go make better.
turns.zh: 是的，这很有趣……我的意思是，我确实认为这家公司比我见过的任何一家公司都更善于吃自己的狗粮，而且每个人都在不断地，我们说 Versel 用 Versel 打造 Versel。所以你总是在寻找方法，嘿，我们如何使用我们的产品来做我们需要做的事情？因此，要么了解客户想要什么，要么了解我们的产品缺少哪些我们可以改进的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along these lines, something that's already come across a lot in the way that you described this stuff is I've heard a lot about how you think about go-to-market as a product. A lot of people listening to this, as I've said, are product builders. So I think this is a really nice way of thinking about go-to-market. I'm guessing you've already talked about elements of this, but just what's a way to think about go-to-market as a product?
turns.zh: 沿着这些思路，我已经听过很多关于您如何看待产品上市的问题。正如我所说，很多听这个的人都是产品开发者。所以我认为这是一种非常好的思考进入市场的方式。我猜您已经讨论过其中的要素，但是如何看待产品进入市场呢？

turns.speaker: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser
turns.en: Yeah, I've always, so I had this realization probably a little over a decade ago in my career. So my first job out of college was working on Gmail in 2004. So Gmail launched on April 1st, I joined on June 1st. And as I'm sure you'll remember as well, Gmail was this incredible innovation, massive JavaScript application that didn't really exist at the time. And it had this gig of storage. It was a full year before Yahoo Mail caught up and even longer before Hotmail and others did. So that was the level of technical differentiation between Gmail and the next best. And a decade later, you had cloud computing enabling folks to do stuff that you never would've been able to do previously. And so I kind of felt like, huh, software's starting to commoditize a little bit. And so when that happens, when technical differentiation kind of narrows, what are other things that will differentiate you? (00:48:01): And I was started thinking outside of tech, we buy a lot of things because of how we feel about them. And so I started to develop this thesis that actually the experience that you have of being sold to will increasingly actually differentiate a company and drive buying decisions if products are only different at the margin. And so if you believe that, then you really want to create a customer buying journey that feels like very unique experiences. And so we did a lot of this at Stripe and now we're looking to replicate this here. But an example of one of the things I think we did really nicely at Stripe was a lot of companies sales, the first call after you're qualified, we've decided you're worth engaging in sales process is discovery, which is basically let me ask you a lot of questions to try to under-uncover paint, figure out where buying power lies, et cetera. (00:49:03): And so that is kind of boring sometimes for a customer. You're basically being quizzed often on the phone. And so what we started to do at Stripe was that first session was a whiteboarding session, and we would actually get together and have you draw your architecture for payments and all the other things that were under the hood to enable you to take money and drive customer outcomes. And through that we would learn a ton about what was in your stack, what we were going to have to compete with, displace where value lied. But the customer also learned a lot themselves because in many cases they'd never drawn their architecture diagram. And so they left that meeting with an asset and a sense of like, "Wow, this is a really collaborative person who's deeply interested in helping me develop a mental model for how to think about this." And then we had other things that we would do. (00:50:00): So that's sort of how I think about building go-to-market-like a product is basically you need to go through from the first time you become aware that the company exists to again, that sort of five-year heavily retained wall-to-wall customer a set of experiences. And those experiences can feel transactional, flat, boring, or they can feel very human, personalized and unique. And so we try to go map those out and figure out how do you bring the product to bear, make it really human, and hopefully that creates a customer for life in the end.
turns.zh: 是的，我一直都是这样，所以我可能在十多年前的职业生涯中就意识到了这一点。我大学毕业后的第一份工作是 2004 年的 Gmail。Gmail 于 4 月 1 日推出，我于 6 月 1 日加入。我相信您也会记得，Gmail 是一项令人难以置信的创新，是当时还不存在的大型 JavaScript 应用程序。它有这么大的存储空间。雅虎邮箱花了整整一年才赶上，甚至比 Hotmail 和其他公司还要早。这就是 Gmail 与次优产品之间的技术差异水平。十年后，云计算使人们能够做以前无法做的事情。所以我觉得，嗯，软件开始商品化了一点。因此，当这种情况发生时，当技术差异化缩小时，还有哪些其他因素可以使您与众不同？ (00:48:01)：我开始思考科技之外的问题，我们购买很多东西是因为我们对它们的感觉。所以我开始发展这个论文，实际上，如果产品只是在边际上有所不同，那么你所拥有的销售经验实际上会越来越使一家公司脱颖而出，并推动购买决策。因此，如果您相信这一点，那么您确实想创建一个感觉非常独特的客户购买旅程。我们在 Stripe 做了很多这样的事情，现在我们希望在这里复制这一点。但我认为我们在 Stripe 做得非常好的一件事的一个例子是很多公司的销售，在你合格后的第一个电话，我们认为你值得参与销售流程是发现，这基本上是让我问你很多问题，试图揭开油漆的真相，弄清楚购买力在哪里，等等。 (00:49:03)：所以有时这对客户来说有点无聊。基本上你经常在电话里被问到。因此，我们在 Stripe 开始做的是，第一场会议是白板会议，我们实际上会聚在一起，让你绘制支付架构和所有其他幕后的东西，使你能够赚钱并推动客户成果。通过这些，我们可以大量了解你的堆栈中有什么，我们将不得不与之竞争，取代价值所在。但客户自己也学到了很多东西，因为在很多情况下他们从未绘制过架构图。因此，他们在离开那次会议时，带着一种资产和一种感觉，“哇，这是一个非常善于合作的人，他非常有兴趣帮助我建立一个如何思考这个问题的心理模型。”然后我们还有其他要做的事情。 (00:50:00)：这就是我对构建进入市场的产品的看法，基本上你需要经历从你第一次意识到公司存在到再次，那种五年大量保留的全方位客户的一系列体验。这些体验可能让人感觉事务性、平淡、无聊，也可能感觉非常人性化、个性化和独特。因此，我们尝试将这些内容绘制出来，并弄清楚如何使产品发挥作用，使其真正人性化，并希望最终能创造出终生客户。

(00:54:39): And then, I don't know if this is a tactic per se, but I do think just a good reminder for founders in particular who are still in that maybe founder-led sales moment is just the value of really good discovery. turns.en: So segmentation is basically how do you carve up the world of companies that exist on the planet to reason about them where they buy differently? So I'll give examples from Stripe and Versel to bring this home. So a very typical company segmentation is small, medium, large. That's a rational way to do things. And that was important for Stripe because it was a consumption-based business. (01:02:10): So if you were going to grow at 200% year-on-year, you were more valuable to Stripe than if you were going to grow at 8% year-on-year. And so we wanted to spend more time, spend more money going after the 200% growers than the 8%. So that was one that informed your strategy on who you targeted.
